deep.reconstruction:
This is page 9 of Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae, Tom. X (for 1764, printed 1766). It is not Euler's paper itself. It is the Latin editorial 'Summarium', an abstract of the volume's contents. The first three lines end the summary of the preceding memoir (section I). That summary closes by saying that 'in all cases the integration is to be regarded as accomplished, so this investigation has brought no small increment to the integral calculus.'

Then comes the joint summary of items II and III: 'Elementa calculi variationum' (E296, p. 51) and 'Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum' (E297, p. 94).

The summary opens historically:
- Even before the famous isoperimetric problem, geometers had published notable examples of this kind.
- The ancients already knew that the circle encloses the largest area among figures of equal perimeter. They inferred this from the nature of the circle.
- They never dared attack the question directly, that is, search among all figures of given perimeter for the one of maximal area. That would require the infinitesimal calculus.
- Once the foundations of that calculus were laid, Johann Bernoulli successfully solved the brachistochrone problem. The page breaks at 'quippe qua / inter', and the next page continues with the cycloid.

In modern terms the page sets up the problem class: extremize a functional (area, descent time) over a space of curves, possibly under an integral constraint (fixed length). This is what Euler's two memoirs treat with the δ-operator. No mathematics is actually carried out on this page.
errors: The summary's history is simplified. Zenodorus (2nd c. BC) did give direct arguments for the polygonal isoperimetric property, so 'never dared attack directly' is an overstatement, though fair for the full continuous problem.

Ordering: the brachistochrone (Johann Bernoulli, 1696) was solved independently by several people (Jakob Bernoulli, Leibniz, Newton, L'Hôpital). Jakob posed the isoperimetric problem in 1697 as a counter-challenge. The summary's framing is standard and conventional rather than wrong.

ideas.what: Historical framing: isoperimetric property of the circle known to the ancients, but no direct extremal method existed before the calculus
ideas.modern_name: Isoperimetric problem / history of the calculus of variations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Zenodorus (partial), later Steiner and Weierstrass (rigorous proofs)
ideas.where_published: Similar historical remarks appear in Euler's Methodus inveniendi (1744) and E296 itself

ideas.what: Brachistochrone as the first problem of the new calculus of variations

deep.surprise_reason: This is an editorial summary page with purely standard historical narrative about the isoperimetric and brachistochrone problems. It contains no mathematics and nothing unrecorded.
transcription_corrections: The page number '9' at top right and the ornamental header ') o (' are omitted from the transcription.
'promotionem' is broken across the line in the original as 'promo-t'onem' (damaged type); the reading 'promotionem' is correct.
The first word 'go' is the tail of 'ergo' carried over from the previous summary page.
